sections.body:
This is a story about Bảo. She is nine years old and she loves drawing animals. She draws dinosaurs every single day.

One morning, her grandfather gives her a folded map. On the map there is a valley with a gate of green ferns. At the bottom it says: Dinosaur Land. Come quietly.

A good adventure has a shape. It has a beginning, a middle and an end. The beginning tells you who is going and why. The middle brings the surprise. The end gives you something worth keeping.

This journey has that shape. At the beginning, Bảo opens the fern gate and the valley is quiet. In the middle, she meets the giants and learns to be very, very still. At the end, she finds something small under a big leaf.

Read it slowly. Then tell it to someone else. That is how an adventure becomes yours.
examples: This story is about a journey into a dinosaur valley.
A good adventure has a beginning, a middle and an end.
I can tell this story again tomorrow.
sections.heading: What this journey is about

sections.body:
The fern gate is taller than Bảo. Its leaves are green and wet and they smell like rain.

She pushes the gate open. It makes a soft swishing sound, like a broom on a floor. She does not shout. She walks in.

The valley is very quiet. Big green leaves cover the ground. Something moves far away, and the leaves shake from the bottom up.

Bảo looks down at her boots. There are round marks in the wet soil. Some are as small as her thumb. Some are bigger than her school bag. She counts them as she walks. Nine small ones. Then one very big one.

Her grandfather's map says: Follow the big prints. They will take you to the heart of the valley.

So Bảo follows them. The prints are cool and soft and they shine a little in the wet. She walks carefully, so she does not step on them.
examples: The fern gate was taller than Bảo.
The leaves shook from the bottom up.
She stepped around the prints so she would not spoil them.
sections.heading: How the journey began

sections.body:
At the heart of the valley there is a clearing of warm sand.

A **dinosaur** is an animal that lived a very long time ago, long before people. Dinosaurs had different shapes. Some were tall like towers. Some were small as a dog.

The first one Bảo sees is slow and green. It has a long neck, and it pulls down leaves from the top of a tree. It eats plants, so it is called a **herbivore**. A herbivore is an animal that eats plants.

Bảo does not move. She counts her breaths. The dinosaur chews, and the small trees shake.

Then the ground thumps. Thump. Thump. A heavy animal comes through the ferns, with a thick tail and small arms. This one eats meat, so it is a **carnivore**. A carnivore is an animal that eats other animals.

Bảo's knees want to run. She does not run. She stands behind a fern and waits.

The heavy animal sniffs the air. It sniffs towards her. Bảo holds her map against her chest and says nothing at all. After a long moment, the animal turns away and walks into the trees.

Stillness saved her. A loud girl would have lost her way home.
examples: The long-necked dinosaur ate leaves, so it was a herbivore.
The ground thumped when the heavy animal walked.
sections.heading: The middle: meeting the giants

sections.body:
On the way back, Bảo stops. A huge leaf has fallen over something small and round.

She lifts the leaf with two fingers. Inside the leaf there is a bone. It is warm, and yellow, and smooth. It is not a new bone. It is a **fossil**. A fossil is the hard part of an animal that turned to stone after a very long time.

Bảo's heart jumps. A fossil like this belongs in a museum. She thinks of her grandfather's shelf, and of the sign she could write for it.

Then she hears footsteps. An old ranger walks into the clearing. He looks at the bone, and then at her.

"You can carry it," he says. "Or you can draw it and leave it."

Bảo asks why. The ranger says a fossil in the ground keeps its family near. Take one home, and the valley gets a little emptier.

So Bảo takes out her notebook. She kneels down and draws the bone, slowly, with all the little lines. When she finishes, she puts the leaf back over it, exactly how it was.

She walks home with a drawing in her notebook and mud on her boots. The drawing is hers. The bone stays in the valley, and the valley stays full.
examples: The fossil was warm, yellow and smooth.
She drew the bone and put the leaf back.
The drawing was hers. The bone stayed in the valley.
sections.heading: The surprise: the small bone under the leaf

sections.body:
These are the words you will meet in this story. Learn them here, and you can use them in your own sentences.

A **dinosaur** is an animal that lived a very long time ago. Dinosaurs are gone now, but their bones are still turning into stone under the ground.

A **fossil** is the hard part of an animal that turned to stone. A fossil tells us what the animal looked like when it was alive.

A **footprint** is the mark a foot leaves in soft ground. Big animals leave big footprints, and they can show us which way the animal walked.

A **herbivore** is an animal that eats plants. A **carnivore** is an animal that eats other animals.

A **valley** is a low piece of land with higher ground on both sides. Rivers often run through valleys, and wild animals like to hide in them.
examples: A fossil is a bone that turned to stone.
A footprint is a mark left in soft ground.
A herbivore eats plants and a carnivore eats animals.
sections.heading: The words inside this story

terms.example: The long-necked dinosaur pulled leaves from the treetop.
terms.gloss: An animal that lived a very long time ago, long before people. Dinosaurs are gone now, but their bones turn to stone under the ground.

terms.example: She found a yellow fossil under a huge leaf.
terms.gloss: The hard part of an animal that turned to stone after a very long time. Fossils tell us what the animal looked like.

terms.example: The footprints pointed deeper into the valley.
terms.gloss: The mark a foot leaves in soft ground. Big animals leave big footprints, and they show which way the animal walked.

terms.example: The tall one was a herbivore, because it ate leaves.
terms.gloss: An animal that eats plants, such as leaves and grass.

terms.example: The heavy animal with the thick tail was a carnivore.
terms.gloss: An animal that eats other animals. Carnivores are often the strong, heavy ones.

sections.body:
What did Bảo learn? She learned that a valley full of giants is kept alive by quiet feet and quiet voices. She also learned that some things are not ours to take.

The bone was hers to draw. It was not hers to carry home. Bảo kept the drawing, and the drawing was enough.

Here is how to tell this adventure to someone. Keep the order, and the surprise will land in the right place.

Start with Bảo and the fern gate. Tell the giants in the middle. Save the bone under the leaf for last. Then say the small lesson in one short sentence.

The lesson of this adventure is this: take the picture, not the thing that belongs to somebody else.
examples: The story starts with Bảo opening the fern gate.
The surprise comes at the very end.
Take the picture, not the thing that belongs to somebody else.
sections.heading: The small lesson, and how to tell the story
steps: Start with the character: Bảo at the fern gate with her grandfather's map.
Tell the middle: the big prints, the quiet clearing and the giants.
Tell the surprise: the fossil under the leaf, and the drawing instead.
End with the lesson: take the picture, not the thing that belongs to somebody else.

item.summary: Bảo walks into a green valley where dinosaurs still walk, and finds something small under a big leaf. Follow her past the ferns, the giant footprints and the warm nests. After reading, you can retell the journey, use five new dinosaur words in your own sentences, and explain why she left the bone in the ground.
item.title: A Journey Through Dinosaur Land
